newsitem.title: USA: US corporate bonds end higher on retail buying.
newsitem.headline: US corporate bonds end higher on retail buying.

text.p: U.S. corporate bonds closed higher on Friday as a result of continued strong institutional investor buying, traders said.

Higher overall interest rates brought new buyers, particularly insurance companies, into the investment grade market, traders said. Spreads of most high-grade bonds tightened by at least one basis point.
"There was an incredible amount of new cash coming from insurance companies today. They like to buy anytime the market backs up because they're looking for yield pickup," said one trader.
In the primary market, Indian petrochemical firm, Reliance Industries Ltd, sold $314 million in Baa3/BB-plus-rated notes on Friday.
The two-part deal consisted of $214 million in 8.25 percent 30-year notes and $100 million in 10.25 percent 100-year notes.
First Union Capital also sold $250 million in 10-year trust preferred securities via Goldman Sachs. The securities were priced at 104 basis points over Treasuries.
In the high-yield market, prices ended unchanged on modest trading volume.
Traders reported that paper-sector junk bonds such as Riverwood International and Crown Paper made back some of the losses they suffered earlier in the week.
Bonds in the supermarket sector, however, dropped by 1/4 a point on continued negative sentiment, with the exception of Safeway Inc.
Safeway bonds rose modestly as Moody's Investors Service Inc upgraded their ratings.

Moody's stated, "the rating actions reflect the steady growth of the company's earnings and cash flow, its strong franchise and the pending acquisition of Vons Companies Inc, a leading Southern Califronia food retailer."

Meanwhile, the long-end of the Treasury market suffered substantial losses on Friday as a result of the release of a stronger-than-expected payroll growth number in December. The 30-year long bond dropped over one point, ending the day at 95-19/32. Its yield rose to 6.85 percent.
